analysis.one_liner: Repeals the main foreign surveillance law and requires warrants before the government spies on Americans.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would require warrants before the government surveils Americans, was introduced with no cosponsors and has sat without action in two House committees.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), the 1978 law that sets the rules for government spying on foreign threats. In its place, it would require federal officers to get a normal court warrant before electronically monitoring an American, searching their property, or targeting them for intelligence purposes. It would also bar the government from using information about an American gathered through the intelligence apparatus — including under Executive Order 12333 or during surveillance of a foreigner — against that person in any proceeding, and it would make warrantless surveillance of Americans a crime punishable by prison time.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans — anyone whose calls, messages, or records could be swept up in intelligence gathering — would gain stronger privacy protections: the government would need an ordinary court warrant to spy on a citizen, and evidence collected outside that rule could not be used against them. Criminal penalties would also give intelligence officers a personal reason to follow the rules.

how_it_helps.text: It would require federal officers to get a warrant from a federal court before electronically surveilling a U.S. citizen, physically searching their property, or targeting them for foreign intelligence collection.
It would bar the government from using, in any proceeding or investigation, information about an American obtained under Executive Order 12333 or picked up during surveillance of a foreigner.
It would make it a crime, punishable by up to five years in prison, for officials to surveil Americans without a warrant or to knowingly use or disclose information gathered that way.

analysis.who_pays: Intelligence agencies and officials conducting foreign surveillance would lose their main legal framework and face criminal liability for warrantless surveillance of citizens; national security officials argue counterterrorism and counterintelligence work would be harder.

drawbacks.text: Repealing FISA entirely would eliminate the existing framework — including the FISA court — that currently authorizes and reviews surveillance of foreign agents and terrorists, with no replacement system provided for gathering foreign intelligence.

National security officials argue that warrant requirements for foreign intelligence collection can slow or block urgent investigations of terrorism and espionage; the bill's criminal penalties of up to five years in prison for intelligence officers could make agencies hesitant to act even where collection is lawful.

Excluding all information about a citizen gathered under Executive Order 12333 or during surveillance of a foreigner from any proceeding could make it harder to prosecute cases where evidence was lawfully collected overseas.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy protections are broad and could matter a lot to anyone swept up in surveillance. But repealing FISA outright, rather than amending it, would also throw away the court-approved framework that (in principle) reviews and limits foreign surveillance, and the bill offers few alternatives for tracking foreign spies and terrorists. Critics would say it swaps a flawed system for no system. The serious drawback is the loss of structured oversight of legitimate foreign intelligence work, alongside the serious gain of warrant requirements and criminal penalties for spying on Americans.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary and Intelligence committees and never moved — no hearings, no markup, no vote — and it has no cosponsors.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 3, 2025 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The action history shows no activity after the referral — no committee vote, no floor action, and no hearing listed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The intelligence community keeps the existing surveillance framework intact for now; ordinary people gain nothing yet, but lose nothing either since the bill never advanced.

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal FISA and require warrants for surveillance of Americans.

against.name: House Intelligence Committee leadership
against.role: Referral committee with jurisdiction over surveillance bills
against.what_they_did: The committee with jurisdiction over FISA took no action on the bill, letting it sit without a hearing or markup.

sides.party_line_note: No votes or cosponsors exist to measure party support; surveillance powers have historically split both parties, and this bill drew no visible backing from either.

industries.industry: Intelligence agencies and the surveillance apparatus
industries.note: FISA repeal plus warrant requirements and criminal penalties would strip the government's main legal authority for foreign surveillance and expose officers to prosecution. The bill was written precisely to shrink this power.

Companies currently face government demands for customer data under FISA authorities; the bill would narrow those demands but not eliminate them. Consumers' communications would be more shielded from government access.

analysis.trajectory: With no cosponsors, no committee action in nearly a year, and referral to the Intelligence Committee — whose members generally defend FISA — the bill is very unlikely to advance in this Congress. It will most likely die quietly when the Congress ends.
